items.title: Inside Elizabeth Holmes’ Secret Oceanfront Rental Seen in ‘You Can See Everything’ Documentary a Month Before She’s Sent to Prison
items.summary:
The Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” takes place in the Theranos founder’s former Del Mar, CA , rental—and the property’s location in an exclusive, gated community could be just part of the reason the film’s unexpected release was such a smash.

The project—which is now available to stream on demand and was directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim —was kept secret for the four years it was in production, leaving viewers in awe after the documentary’s surprise Sept. 6 premiere at Telluride Film Festival.

Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans , invited the film crew—which Oppenheim told Variety was intentionally kept intimate to keep the project a secret—to reside in the guesthouse of the home for the 34 days before she reported to Federal Prison Camp in Bryan, TX , on May 30, 2023.

“Keeping it under wraps was very important because we never wanted to get in front of what we were capturing,” the director shared.

The crew would typically shoot for 16-hour days, with Fielder telling Variety that cameras were strategically positioned to “cover the whole house” so nothing would be missed.

Directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim worked tirelessly to keep the film's creation "under wraps." (JC Olivera/Getty Images) 

The documentary takes place in Elizabeth Holmes' ultraprivate rental in an exclusive and gated community in Del Mar, CA. (Google Earth) 

The community has only about a dozen residences and is guarded around the clock. (Google Earth)

items.title: Derek Hough Recalls Difficult Utah Upbringing with Neighbors Who ‘Terrorized’ Family Before Moving to London
items.summary:
Derek Hough is opening up about his upbringing, sharing painful details from his childhood in his new Hulu documentary, “The Symphony of Dance.”

In the film, the “Dancing with the Stars" judge returns to his childhood home in Utah , and details the challenging environment he was raised in.

“The neighborhood that we grew up in, we definitely just had some neighbors that weren’t great,” Derek, 41, explained. “They pretty much terrorized my family in a lot of ways.”

“They hung me up in a tree by my ankles. They put a gun to my head, spat on me, hogtied me up in a field and left me there,” he continued. “One of my neighbors was, for lack of a better word, really inappropriate with me, physically.”

Eventually, Derek’s parents separated, and the family moved across town to an apartment building where his mother and father lived in units across the hall from one another.

Derek Hough is opening up about his challenging childhood in the new Hulu documentary, "The Symphony of Dance." (Disney via Getty Images) 

The biographical film unpacks Derek's past, as well as wife Hayley Erbert Hough's life-changing brain injury. (Disney via Getty Images)

“I just didn’t understand where I was going. I didn’t understand what I was doing,” he said. “I was just kind of left to my own devices as a 12-year-old. I would skip school. I would skip dance, just floating around with no direction.”

items.title: Can a Solar Generator Actually Keep Your Lights On During an Outage—or Is It Just Expensive Hype?
items.summary:
Winter storm season is fast approaching, with even Thanksgiving being primed for power outages across the country. 

If you’d like to limit its disruption on your everyday life, generators may be top of mind.

As you do your research, you may come across solar generators and wonder how they compare to other options.

“A solar generator uses sunlight as its fuel. It also happens to be clean, quiet, and quick,” explains Ben Zook , founder and owner of Belmont Solar , a solar installation company in Gordonville, PA . 

While a solar generator will likely be more expensive upfront, it could be a smart investment, depending on your location and goals. 

By understanding how it works as well as its limitations, you can decide whether it’s the right backup solution for your home .

What is a solar generator? 

The name “solar generator” is a bit misleading. 

This device is actually a portable battery system you can refill with solar panels and use when you don’t have power. 

It includes a built-in inverter that converts DC electricity into AC electricity, which most household appliances use. In addition, it might come with USB ports to charge electronic devices such as cellphones. 

So, how does the recharging process work?

“Put simply, solar panels convert sunlight into electricity. When sunlight hits the panels, it produces an electric current,” explains Fox Swim , senior industry researcher at Aurora Solar in Nanaimo, British Columbia .

Keep in mind that a solar generator doesn’t provide unlimited power. It’s limited by your battery’s capacity and how much electricity your…
items.t: Can a Solar Generator Actually Keep Your Lights On During an Outage—or Is It Just Expensive Hype?

items.title: Condo vs. Townhouse: Which Investment Will Turn Around More Equity After a Decade?
items.summary:
Between 2014 and 2024, the difference in price appreciation between condos and single-family homes was less than 5 percentage points nationally, according to an analysis from Realtor.com® . Townhouses came even closer to matching the performance of detached homes—trailing by just 0.8 percentage points.

It's a remarkable outcome for the buyers opted out of the which picket fence dream, and instead invested in properties that often offer a more affordable entry point into homeownership. But that outcome may be harder to replicate in today's rapidly changing housing market.

Condo values fell 0.8% year over year in August 2026, even as single-family home values rose 1.8%, according to data from Intercontinental Exchange . And as home price growth cools, expenses that were easier to stomach during years of rapid appreciation stand to take a bigger bite out of homeowners' returns.

Even so, those national numbers tell only part of the story. In some regions, condos substantially outperformed townhouses over the decade examined by Realtor.com, challenging the notion that owning a piece of land necessarily leads to stronger appreciation.

Understanding what drove those differences—and how the economics of owning each property type are changing—offers some clues as to where buyers might find the greatest opportunity to build equity over the next decade.

Neck-and-neck appreciation nationally 

Single-family homes appreciated 87.3% from 2014 to 2024, according to Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones . Townhomes nearly matched that pace at 86.5%, while condos trailed only…
items.t: Condo vs. Townhouse: Which Investment Will Turn Around More Equity After a Decade?

AnnaLynne McCord was still processing a call about her finances when her phone rang again. This time, it was the casting director of “Days of Our Lives” with a job offer.

In an interview with Hollywood Hills Magazine , the actress, 39, said joining the soap “saved” her. McCord had spent five seasons starring on “90210” after appearing on “Ugly Betty” and “Greek.” 

By 2024, when the “Days” offer came along, she was worried about how she would cover her bills.

“I was told that I could not pay my credit cards. You work in this industry, and it’s sobering because you can be at the highest highs, and then things shift,” McCord told the magazine.

McCord said she had devoted much of her time to charity work. That morning, she found herself asking a question about her own future: “Am I going to be okay?”

AnnaLynne McCord was still processing a call about her finances when her phone rang again. This time, it was the casting director of “Days of Our Lives” with a job offer. (JOCE/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images) 

“That afternoon, Marnie, the casting director of Days of our Lives , called me asking if I want to come on the show, and I said, ‘Yes, I do’, in more ways than she would ever know,” McCord recalled.

Looking back, McCord described that call as a “foundational moment of what Days would go on to offer me.” The job came along when she needed the work. 

What surprised her over time was how much the people she worked with would come to mean to her.

“I feel at home here. I feel family here. I feel that people genuinely care about your well-being,” she told Hollywood Hills…

items.title: National Home Value Growth Holds Steady, Yet Miami Outperforms
items.summary:
National growth in home values was flat month over month in September as mortgage rates accelerated and inflation continued running hot. 

The value of single-family homes as measured by repeat transactions increased 2.1% year over year, same as in August, according to data from the  S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index  released on Tuesday.

However, home values fell in real terms for the 16th consecutive month, as September's 3.7% inflation rate outpaced the home value gain by roughly 1.6 percentage points, up from about 1.3 points in August.

"Nominal home prices remain resilient, but inflation is once again widening the gap between nominal and real housing returns," says Rebecca Kaufman , associate director of commodities at S&P Dow Jones Indices.

Across the 20 cities tracked by the index,  Chicago  yet again led the U.S. with a 6.9% annual gain. New York City  took second place with a year-over-year increase of 5.8%, but Miami emerged as the month's surprise, finishing third with a 4.6% gain.

"Miami’s rise is particularly notable," points out Kaufman. "After moving into fourth place among the 20 cities in July and August, it has now climbed into the top three, a sharp reversal from its comparatively weak performance in 2025."

(Realtor.com) 

On the other side of the spectrum, Seattle recorded the largest annual decline for the fourth consecutive
month at 1.9%, followed by Denver (-1.0%) and Dallas (-0.9%), reflecting a persistent regional divergence. 

September also revealed a widening gap between seasonal weakness and underlying price momentum. On a nonseasonally…
items.t: National Home Value Growth Holds Steady Yet Miami Outperforms

items.title: Mom and Dad Survived 1980s Mortgage Rates. Here Is Why Buying a Home Today Is Still Much Harder.
items.summary:
It now takes the typical household 10.5 years to save for a down payment on a home —more than triple the time it took in the 1980s, according to a new analysis from Realtor.com® .

It's a stark generational divide that may be hard to ignore this Thanksgiving. Roughly 1 in 3 young adults lived with their parents in 2025—a record 25.2 million Americans aged 18 to 34—according to separate research from Realtor.com . And the share rising the fastest is in regions long considered affordability havens.

For families sharing a roof, one seemingly innocent question could spark a much thornier conversation than intended: When are you going to buy a house? 

For parents who bought their first homes in the 1980s, the question might seem fair. After all, mortgage rates reached a record 18.63% in 1981, while inflation averaged 13.5% in 1980— compared to 7.28% and 3.7% , respectively, today.

But while older generations certainly faced obstacles of their own, those war stories don't fully capture the economics of today's market, says Hannah Jones , senior economist at Realtor.com .

“The reality is that today's aspiring buyers face a different housing market than generations before,” she explains. “While mortgage rates were significantly higher in the 1980s, home prices were far more attainable relative to household incomes, allowing buyers to save for a down payment in a fraction of the time it takes today.”

Why mortgage rates are only part of the story 

The impulse to look back at the 1980s for perspective on today's housing market is certainly understandable. But to Jones' point,…
items.t: Mom and Dad Survived 1980s Mortgage Rates. Here Is Why Buying a Home Today Is Still Much Harder.

items.title: Inside a Plan To Convert Shipping Containers From the Border Wall Into Affordable Housing
items.summary:
Flying over the Arizona desert one day in 2023, Beau Phillips looked out his plane window and spotted thousands of shipping containers —remnants of a dismantled border wall—scattered across the arid landscape.

That chance glimpse sparked an idea: convert the abandoned steel boxes into hundreds of affordable housing units and build a whole new community in the Tucson area for some of the 40,000 low-income residents waiting for housing assistance .

"These were built to keep people out, and now we're welcoming people in," Phillips tells Realtor.com® . "There is a poetic justice there."

Phillips, a semiretired MTV Networks and radio marketing executive, first encountered the containers in late 2022, when he took part in a demonstration protesting then-Arizona Gov. Doug Ducey 's order to install a border barrier made up of more than 2,000 double-stacked steel shipping crates, topped with wire, near Yuma and in the Coronado National Forest.

After the Biden administration and environmental groups successfully sued, arguing that the 10-mile wall of containers was illegally placed on federal and tribal land, the state took the barrier apart in early 2023. 

Some 2,200 steel boxes were left in the desert with no plan for their disposal, until Phillips saw them from a plane and pitched state officials on a new use for them.

To bring his vision to life, Phillips founded a nonprofit, Boxes of Hope , and teamed up with La Frontera AZ , a major affordable housing developer and behavioral health provider, to create a village made up of 350 to 450 shipping containers transformed into…
items.t: Inside a Plan To Convert Shipping Containers From the Border Wall Into Affordable Housing

items.title: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee
items.summary:
These ancient and often grossly unfair taxes are stifling the economy and young people. It’s long past time for radical reform

When voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first, council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax.

Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan. Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

items.title: Flipping a House Isn’t Paying Like It Used To. Is Renting the Better Bet?
items.summary:
The typical home flip generated just $60,526 in gross profit in the second quarter of 2026, down from $71,000 a year earlier, according to new data—before accounting for renovation costs or other expenses.

It's a shrinking cushion for investors who have long relied on a simple formula to fuel their business: Buy low , apply elbow grase, and sell high. But with elevated borrowing costs and renovation expenses eating into margins, there's much less room than there used to be for anything to go wrong.

The report, from real estate data analytics company ATTOM , found that flipping returns have been declining for two years, with the typical gross return falling to 21.5%, from 27.6% a year earlier.

"Flippers are still making money in most markets, but the typical return continues to narrow," Rob Barber , CEO of ATTOM, said via press release. "The second-quarter numbers continue the general downward trend in profit margins and gross profits we have seen over the past two years."

So, why not skip the resale altogether and rent out the property instead?

After all, the promise of passive income—collecting rent every month while building equity—helped fuel a wave of small investors buying up homes earlier this decade when borrowing costs were low and rents were on a meteoric rise.

But the economics have changed for landlords, too.

Potential rental yields declined in more than half of U.S. counties with comparable data between 2025 and 2026, according to separate ATTOM research . That's to say nothing of the work involved in managing a rental property, which, as Realtor.com®…
items.t: Flipping a House Isn’t Paying Like It Used To. Is Renting the Better Bet?

items.title: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul Signs New Private Listings Bill
items.summary:
New York has signed a new private listings bill, which means that properties will be required to be visible to the public as they hit the market unless the seller signs an informed opt-out consent.

Late last week, Gov. Kathy Hochul signed the Fair and Transparent Real Estate Listing Act . The language of the bill requires that real estate listings be marketed in "at least one other publication, platform or website that does not require payment" or for the consumer to work with the brokerage for access.

This follows a quick path through the state's Legislature, which approved the act in a noncontroversial vote in June. The New York State Association of Realtors® strongly supports the bill.

This becomes the latest crackdown on private listings, where a real estate agent markets a property to a limited list of buyers before making it public.

Fair housing advocates say private listings raise discrimination concerns. One study from Bright MLS found private listings take longer to sell and don't guarantee more money.

The listing must be accessible to the general public, "without limitation to a particular brokerage, franchise or select group of licenses." Also, there can't be restrictions on some or all of the details in the listing, according to the language of the bill.

The bill doesn't require a seller or lister to hold open houses or public showings if it violates any state or federal laws related to health and safety. And sellers can opt out, by signing a form that explicitly warns them that the listing will have limited visibility and possible impact on the price…
items.t: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul Signs New Private Listings Bill

items.title: Buying a Home Soon? This Overlooked Open Enrollment Perk Could Save You Thousands in Legal Fees
items.summary:
Buying a home comes with enough expenses already. Between inspections , title insurance , closing costs, and a stack of paperwork that seems to grow every day, it's easy to lose track of what you're paying for.

But what if your employer could help cover some of the legal bills?

It's a possibility many homebuyers may overlook during open enrollment, when employees are typically comparing health insurance premiums and retirement benefits rather than thinking about hiring a lawyer.

Employer-sponsored legal plans, offered through companies such as LegalShield , MetLife and ARAG , can provide access to attorneys for a modest monthly fee.

A real estate attorney can review a purchase agreement, make sure inspection and financing contingencies actually protect the buyer, check the deed and title, examine mortgage documents, and represent a buyer at closing. Depending on the plan, some or all of that may be covered.

Jago Gavin , a LegalShield representative who works with employer groups, tells Realtor.com® that the real value is having someone to consult before signing something you might not fully understand.

"The law is not logical; it's legal," Gavin says.

That's relevant when buying a house , where an unfamiliar contract provision can have expensive consequences.

Gavin recalls a LegalShield member whose attorney spotted a potentially unfavorable mediation clause in real estate paperwork and recommended changing it before the buyer signed.

The potential savings can run from hundreds to thousands of dollars. But there's a catch: Not all legal plans offer the same…
items.t: Buying a Home Soon? This Overlooked Open Enrollment Perk Could Save You Thousands in Legal Fees

items.title: Why an Uninsulated Garage Can Wreak Havoc on Your Home This Winter
items.summary:
An uninsulated garage might seem like no big deal, but come the winter months, it can do more harm than good. 

In fact, when a garage lacks proper insulation during the colder months, frozen pipes, heat loss, and damaged items are bound to arise. 

Fortunately, insulation solutions and preventive measures can help you avoid these issues while protecting your garage, your car, and your home . 

Risks of uninsulated garages during the winter 

An uninsulated garage in the winter months can cause a chain reaction of issues to the home itself. One of the most common risks is frozen pipes. 

“When the plumbing or water lines located in the garage get exposed to below-freezing temps, they may freeze and cause water damage,” explains Chris Boyle , in-house repair tech at Parts Town Home and Fix.com in Nova Scotia . 

Additionally, improperly insulated garages can prompt heat loss throughout the entire home. 

“Many poorly insulated garages share foundations with homes. As a result, cold air may circulate through the living spaces and force families to turn up their heating systems,” says Boyle.

Not only does this put a strain on HVAC systems, it can also drive up monthly heating bills. 

Plus, poor insulation may damage items stored in the garage, particularly car batteries, which can lose charge or fail completely. 

Winterizing your garage can save you more money than you might imagine. (Getty Images) 

How to tell if your garage is insulated

items.t: Why an Uninsulated Garage Can Wreak Havoc on Your Home This Winter

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith 's $42 million Los Angeles property went up in flames after their shed caught fire. 

The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department and the Malibu/Lost Hills Sheriff’s Station responded to a 911 call at the property in the early hours of Nov. 23. 

Officials told People that they arrived to discover a "structure fire" at the couple's Calabasas home . They added that no one was hurt.

“It appears a shed caught fire, and the cause is believed to be accidental,” the statement from the sheriff's department revealed. 

In audio from the 911 call obtained from Page Six, firefighters can be heard saying, "We do have a shed on fire with no spread to the brush."

An emergency personnel noted that they were already "on scene," and then another firefighter explained that the fire had been "downgraded to a structure."

The couple's Calabasas property serves as their primary residence. Set on 150 acres, the estate—which they began working on in 1997, the same year they tied the knot—features high-end amenities, including a basketball court, a tennis court, and a massive swimming pool.

Trophy properties—those priced $10 million and above—made up half the contracts signed last week, leading the luxury market into the second biggest year in two decades, according to Olshan Realty . 

As of Nov. 22, an impressive 294 contracts were signed at $10 million and above, not far off the peak year of 2021, when 400 were signed. The average asking price for last week was $10.5 million, and properties were moving with a fairly low 5% average discount. 

Corcoran's Deborah Grubman , who co-listed last week's most expensive sale—a $28.75 million triplex in the Pritzker Prize–winning Richard Meier building in the West Village—says that the luxury market normally shows signs of slowing down around the Thanksgiving holiday. But not this year.

"New York is still a very desirable destination for people of wealth," she tells Realtor.com® .

The glass triplex at 176 Perry St.—one of the city's most coveted blocks—was owned by Broadway and movie star Hugh Jackman . The condo, built in 2001, had been on and off the market since June 2022, and at one point was priced at $39 million.

items.title: New Homes Are Now $40K Cheaper Than Existing Homes
items.summary:
New-construction homes are less expensive than existing ones, and the difference has never been larger, the National Association of Home Builders has found.

Last month's NAHB/Wells Fargo Cost of Housing Index found the median new-home price is $393,300, compared to a median-priced existing home, which comes to $432,900 in the third quarter of 2026. That's the largest difference between new- and existing-home prices in the history of NAHB's tracking, Chairman Bill Owens said.

Builders, struggling to find buyers, are digging deeper to offer incentives on new homes. The  National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index  plunged to a 14-year low last week. Many of the nation's major homebuilders have reported large year-over-year declines in revenue. But housing starts continue apace , showing some hope for the market long term.

“Builders are working with buyers to make new homes more affordable and appealing in a tough market, yet the latest CHI data show housing costs still overburden families,” NAHB Chief Economist Robert Dietz said in a statement.

A typical family would have to pay 36% of their income for a median-priced existing home. They'd need 33% of their income for a new home, a drop of 1% from the second quarter. And that accounts for a $17,000 drop in the median new-home price in the second quarter, when it was $434,900, NAHB found.

items.t: New Homes Are Now $40K Cheaper Than Existing Homes
